utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you gave to tell the truth still applies today. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before we continue with cross-examination, could we please see the sketch drawn by the witness which is P828, if I'm not mistaken. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, you spoke about the Muslim priest in your evidence. You said his name was Rifat Neziraj tell me please, is this man still alive?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where does he live and work nowadays?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He continues to live in the old village. He is now an elderly man, no longer working.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell us when he informed about the killing of the Zeka family: Habib, Faruk, and Hemo. Did he tell you how he had come to know about that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he came to my house, he found me in the yard, and I noticed that he looked extremely worried. I asked him what was wrong with him, and he said Bajram, They killed Emin and his two sons. I said, Please, maybe it's not true, let not the others hear this because they -- everybody will panic. Please don't say this, it may not be true. But he said, Yes, it is. In fact, Hadja, the mom lives beyond -- a bit beyond the Zeka family, and he said that he was coming from there, he said that everything was true. I asked him whether he told anybody else, and he said, Yes, I told another neighbour. And I, in fact, tried to keep it hidden so that people wouldn't panic. In fact, the news had been spreading around very, very quickly. And as I said later, at around 1.00 people started converging out of fear. And that's the way everything occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was it your impression that Rifat was an eye-witness, or is it something that you don't know anything about?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he had not been an eye-witness to the murder, but he had been in proximity to the Zeka family and spoken to his family members, and it was they who told him that the murder had occurred on the night before, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have here your sketch, but not the last version that was admitted into evidence where you marked the houses with an A and a B, the houses of the Zeka family. I think that is Exhibit P127. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please zoom in the one D127 with an A and a B. Just that one, please. We don't need the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, please tell me in which house did Emin and his two sons Habib and Faruk live? You said that the Zeka family lived in two houses, now, in which of those two houses Emin lived with his two sons, and where did this happen?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emin and his two sons lived in this place marked by a B, whereas the murder happened on the other side where the families had been converged. Because as I said before, families tried to group together in support of each other and out of fear too. So the murder occurred at the house of the neighbour on the other side at the house of someone called Halit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What was Halit's last name?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, the surname was Fazliu. I'm not entirely sure, but I think it was Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you draw on this sketch the location of his house, and could you mark it with a C, please.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's approximately here, in between the two Zeka families on the opposite side of the road in between the two family compounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So this is where the people assembled; right? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they went to Halit's house. As I was told, it was approximately 30 people who had gathered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, tell me, please, did you hear something about the circumstances surrounding the murder? We heard from you that you had heard that it was three paramilitaries who had committed the murders, but can we hear it from you now given that there were so many witnesses there. What did you hear from them?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, I heard it from people who survived this murder. The other sons of Emin who are alive to this day, and the head of the family Halit who was also present. They told me that at about five to 8.00 when the electricity was cut, three paramilitaries entered and as people were seated they were ordered to kneel and without any further warning they started shooting each one of them using a pistol. Emin and two sons said that he was intent on continuing the executions, but at that stage somebody called Mile entered and said "Stop it now; are you going to kill everyone?" And that's how he stopped. One of Emin's son raised his head to see what was happening, and at that stage he got hit by the butt of the automatic rifle and fainted, and this happened in the presence of his mother. However, he was able to survive. The other three, those who were killed, were left behind, but they returned half an hour later and ordered the family -- took the bodies away and told them to clean up the place so that nobody would be able to learn what had happened, and these three bodies have yet to be retrieved. Nobody knows where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand you. Who removed the three bodies?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bodies were taken by the perpetrators of the murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who lived in the house marked with B?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the house marked with a B lived Emin and his sons, as well as his close family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that you said, yes, they lived in the B house. And who lived in the house marked with A?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the house marked with an A, there were the Zeka cousins of Emin, Hasan and his sons, as well as Aslan along with his wife and his children. They are all with the surname of Zeka, they are relatives of Emin's.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was it Hasan and Safete Zeka who lived in that house and Hasan's wife Fatime? Are these the people that you said went missing and were later found mutilated? Is that the people that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to them. There's four people who were kidnapped by the same paramilitary forces after the murder. So they went after the murder and took Hasan and Aslan alongside their wives; they were kidnapped. And at the end of the war, about two months after the end of the war, but I can't be certain about the date, they were found massacred and mutilated in the Prelez quarters where the headquarters of the military forces were located. The bodies were found in a cesspit, mutilated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to Hasan, Aslan, and their wives; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify something else. What happened to Safete?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Safete was Aslan's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It seemed to me that you mentioned that name in addition to there being a woman called Safete, it seemed to me that you mentioned that there was also a son called Safete, but I seem to have misunderstood you. Thank you. Did you eye-witness the murder of any member of the Zeka family?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see the murder of these members with my own eyes, but there are people who live to this day who were eye-witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, now that you were mentioning eye-witnesses, you said that it was Halit Fazliu in whose house people gathered. Now, can you give me any other names of those 30 who were present at the location where this took place?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of them was Halit, the owner of the house, with all his family, all his family members. I don't know how many there were. I know that he lives in the UK at the moment. But his whole family was there. And then we have Emin's wife, the mother of his sons, and then Emin's brother who lives to this day, and a large number of other family members who are also alive, then Hasan's and Aslan's children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, yes, I understood what you were describing, but I wanted you to give us some names in addition to Halit Fazliu's name. Just give us some other names, first and last names.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say because Halit Fazliu's family has left the place about ten years ago. They don't live there. I'm saying that it's his wife, his sons. Then Emin's sons, and then Hasan's and Aslan's sons too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have understood that. If you don't know the names, that's fine. Just tell me that you can't enumerate any other names and it will be fine. I wanted to hear the name of at least one son of the Zeka family who lives there, or the name of the wife, if you know.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry. Of course I know the name, I just recall it -- I can't recall it just now, but if it were to come to me, I will mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu. Tell me, please, how did it come about that it was decided that all, absolutely all residents should leave the village and go towards Urosevac? How did this come about?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it earlier that after learning that Emin and his two sons had been murdered, people got really worried. And in addition to the torture and the intimidation by the paramilitary forces as well as the murders, there was nothing left to do but to try and flee our homes. As I said it earlier, my own house is in the middle of the village, which means that that's where people converged on, but I've seen people instinctively converge there in a meadow right in front of it. And at that stage even my late wife said, Bajram, what are we waiting for? At which point I told her, Take the children and join the other people. I could not leave my elderly mother alone, so I decided to stay and I did stay a while with my mother, whilst my wife and children joined the crowd. And they proceeded in a valley near my house with the whole crowd instinctively. It was a very short interval during which everybody in the village decided to abandon their homes. I stayed for a period of about two and a half hours or so. However, after pressure from my mother saying, Please go my dear son because they will kill you if they were to find you, I relented and took a bicycle and went and joined my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you told your wife and children to leave the village and to go with the other people, I take that that was your decision for the reasons that you gave. But as for the entire village, who took that decision because it was an organised effort, and it couldn't be that everybody all of a sudden got the same idea in their heads to go to Urosevac? Now, who organised this because it involved some 600 residents or so?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said entirely that I'm not aware of who might have organised it. In fact, I remain convinced that nobody did it. I'm quite sure that it was out of fear, just news of a murder sufficed for everybody to take the decision to go and save himself and their children. I don't think there was any organisation whatsoever. I think it was out of instinct that people started gathering together and fleeing away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, you told us, and you testified about the ugly events involving Serbian forces preceding this event, not only in your village but throughout Kosovo. You said you watched foreign news and TV programs, heard various testimonies, and heard KLA members speak on tell vision. Where did the villagers get the idea they would be safer in Urosevac than in their own village where the same Serbian forces in Urosevac like in Gnjilane, like in Pec, and throughout Kosovo? Where did they get the idea they would be safe somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, we thought our village was one of the safest place, because we had many neighbours who were Serbs. And we had spoken to our Serbian neighbours who had reassured us that nothing was going to happen to us. So you stay behind and nothing is going to happen to us. So that's what we thought in our village. And as a matter of fact, two of my cousins from Ferizaj came and stayed in my village, i.e., before these military forces entered. They stayed there for four to five days, again thinking that our village was safer on account of the mixed population. We thought it was a safe place. That was the reason why I did not abandon our village. However, after what occurred, there was no other option left open to us but to leave the village, and we had no other outlet but towards Ferizaj. At that stage, I knew that there were trains running even though I know that there are people were not able to take the trains and there were families who were left in Ferizaj and the surrounding areas. However, the majority of these people from the village, as I said it earlier, did board these trains and this way left Ferizaj and Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You did say that. I want to know why you thought Urosevac was safer than your village, or any other place in Kosovo for that matter?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, at that stage we were not seeking out safer places as such, what happened is that people instinctively left their own village. What we thought, however, was that should we be forced to flee our villages, and we had made preparation with our tractors and so on and so forth, we had made plans to leave our own homes and proceed towards either Macedonia or Albania. The Biba and Sojeve villages which are next to our village in fact had been emptied by these forces at this stage, so we were fully prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but still, you left the village on your own. You did not do it on direct orders from members of any Serbian unit either regular army, paramilitary, volunteer, or other. You said you got up and left instinctively. It's hard for me to believe, though, that 600 people left just like that, instinctively, without any organisation. Therefore, I ask you again, and please tell me, did any of the Serb forces that I just mentioned drive you out of your village or made you leave by direct orders? I don't mean the instigation in the form of incidents of killings and such, because that happened throughout Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not given any order to leave the village. On the contrary, these forces had told us not to leave the village. They told us to stay there with them just in case Clinton decided to use his infantry in Kosova. They said that we would serve as their protection from these infantry forces. So it was quite the contrary. They said to us that you are not allowed to leave. You will stay here with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If that is so, if there had been these killings you talk about that had started, then how did you manage to leave the village despite this explicit prohibition by the Serbian paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, it is surprising. As I said, some people had remained in the village. I personally thought that these forces would capture these people. And I was quite surprised how these people were not noticed by the forces. As I said, there's a valley, there are meadows around my house, so I really don't know how it happened that the forces didn't see these people who had remained behind. When I passed by these houses where the forces were stationed with my bike, I thought I would be stopped by them and captured by them. I passed by with my bike. The gate was open. I could see the forces there in the courtyard of that house drinking. I really would not be able to say whether they didn't see me or they decided not to stop me. That I don't know. But I just passed there, I saw them in the courtyard, and proceeded towards my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you not very afraid to send away your wife and children in such a situation, what made you send away -- your women and children away while believing that all of you who stayed behind would be arrested and God knows what else?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you that everything happened very fast. My wife, as soon as she saw people gathering there and fleeing, she said to me, What are we waiting for? And that's when I told her to get the children ready and join the crowd. I couldn't personally leave my old and sick mother behind, so I just told her to leave with the children. I said to her, If God's willing, we will see each other again. It all happened very fast. There's no time to do any thinking. This is the reality prevailing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Still I do not quite understand the motives that drove everyone in this combination of circumstances, but let it be, I will not question you anymore about it. Tell me, how many people left the village at that time, and how many stayed?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, about 500 or 600 people left the village that day. Some two or three families that lived near the headquarters of these Chetnik forces remained in the village. I don't know why, whether they didn't dare leave because of the forces or they decided to stay there, but as I said, the rest of the village left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How many people stayed approximately, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in addition to the Serb families that remained in the village, they did not leave the village, they remained there. There were three or four Albanian families that lived near the headquarters of the forces. Maybe altogether 30 or 40 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Including Serbs, or only Albanians? 30 or 40 Albanians? I want to know about the ethnic Albanian population that stayed in the village.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there were three or four Albanian families that remained in the village with a total of 30 or 40 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's clearer now. Mr. Bucaliu, did you know any of the people among the paramilitaries in the village? We are talking about the period from the 2nd of April onwards. From the 2nd of April you were talking about the regular army and then later those people who presented themselves as paramilitaries appeared. Did you know any of those men? Would they have been, perhaps, from Urosevac or some of the villages around? Did you recognise anyone among those men?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, personally, I didn't know any of them. They were unfamiliar faces to me. They stated themselves that they came from Sombor and Vojvodina. They were paramilitary forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We heard that, let's not waste time on something we know. You told us that around 1.000 Albanians lived in the village before 1999. Tell me, how many ethnic Albanians live now in Staro Selo? Is it the same number? Higher? Lower?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There hasn't been a census, so I can only give you an approximate figure. Some families have left, some others have settled in the village, so more or less it's the same figure, about 1.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Talking about your village, you said Serbs and Montenegrins did not return to Staro Selo, they no longer live there. Do you know the reason? Did you ever hear from any of your former neighbours?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when I went back after the war, I didn't see my Serb neighbours there. They had already left. I returned quite late to Kosova on the 6th of July. I learned that they had left in various directions. I do have contacts with them every now and then. We speak on the phone. And they said that the reason why they don't want to come back is because they don't feel comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about their houses? Are they undamaged, unopened, unlooted?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of one house which was next to my house, the remaining were demolished, were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And that happened after June 1999; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard. As I said, when I went back to my village, the Serb families were no longer there. I learned that their houses were demolished after 12th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, when we are talking about these paramilitaries, these volunteers, whatever you call them, the Serbian-Chetnik movement, the radicals, you say they were present in your village and that at the same time there were olive-green tanks. However in the supplemental statement you gave to this Tribunal in August 2006, you say you don't remember that you had ever stated in your statement of 1999 that you had seen tanks. I have read the transcripts of all the previous cases, and I didn't notice that any of my colleagues had asked you about that, but I would like you to clarify.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I didn't understand your question. As I mentioned yesterday, I hear two voices in the background. So I have difficulty sometimes to understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand you perfectly, because I have the same problem myself very often. I will speak more slowly. I said that speaking of the paramilitaries in 1999, you mentioned that at the same time there were tanks present, green tanks. However, in your supplemental statement from 2006, you said you don't remember mentioning tanks being present in the village at the same time as the paramilitaries. I'm asking you now what is correct, what you said in 2006 or that tanks were there in the village at the same time as the paramilitaries? Which of the two is true?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that the paramilitaries didn't have tanks. I heard that there were tanks in Prelez neighbourhood where their headquarters was. The tanks had been hidden. It is true that after the war we came across tanks that had been destroyed there in Prelez neighbourhood. The paramilitaries in the village didn't have tanks. They used civilian cars, but they didn't have tanks. It is true, however, that there were tanks stationed up there in Prelez neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It's true that you mentioned tanks when you said that the Serbian regular army took over the village; we've discussed that before. So now we have a completely clear picture. There were no tanks in the possession of the paramilitary formations; they did not use them. Let me ask you something else: Who is the person you refer to as Captain Sima? Who is he?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Sima, in my opinion, was member of the regular army. He was stationed in the headquarters in Prelez neighbourhood. I believe that there were regular forces stationed there too. This is my assumption based on Sima who resembled a person belonging to the regular forces. An officer from the regular military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how you describe him. Did anyone have any problem, any unpleasantness directly from him? You or anyone else in the village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Personally, I didn't suffer any problems from him, and I didn't hear that others suffered any problems from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, who is Musa, the notorious Muslim?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Musa and Mila were members the paramilitary forces and called themselves leaders of these forces. I think that Musa was a pseudonym that he used. He looked terrible. He would say that he was a butcher who enjoyed slaughtering people. Mile or Mila was thinner than Musa. Together they would roam about in the village and declare themselves as leaders of the paramilitary [Realtime transcript read in error "family-tree"] group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard that Musa killed anyone in the village by slitting their throat, or did anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that he slaughtered anyone, but I did see him slaughtering animals with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I talked to you about the people, you said that he slaughtered and cut up, carved up a bull very professionally so he must have been a butcher. Now, about this captain, you said he intercepted these three men outside of Halit Fazliu's house, that is, in the space between the three houses. He stopped them from doing what they had set out to do. You say he was present at the time. And then you somehow link him up with the fact that when Aslan and his wife and the other person whose name I forget now who were later found mutilated, you say, near Prelez, you somehow link Mile with that. Do you have specific knowledge that Mile was involved in the liquidation of the remainder of the Zeka family?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any specific knowledge that Mile was involved. The survivors who were there when it all occurred told me that they had recognised Mile, that is to say, that after sometime Mile entered there and said to the others, Stop, do you want to kill them all? So in a way, Mile saved the lives of the surviving people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, things are much clearer now. You said also the trenches were being dug by young men on the orders of the paramilitaries. You said it had something to do with preparations for the ground attack about NATO. You said that happened when the paramilitaries first came into the village. Did the paramilitaries come to the village on several occasions? What do you mean we you say they first arrived? Did they come and then go away and then come back again? Because that's not quite clear from that part of your statement. I'm talking about your statement from 1999, 10, 11 -- sorry, paragraphs 9 through 12. When you say "when the paramilitaries first came," does that mean there were other arrivals?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it is stated there. I didn't say when they first came. They were there the whole time. They came on the 5th of April, and were there until we left. Maybe there was a misunderstanding. Maybe I said "when I first came across them." But as for the forces, I can tell you that they were there the whole time, from the 5th of April when they settled there until the time we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Bucaliu, there is no more misunderstanding now. Everything is clear. In paragraph 18 of your 1999 statement, you mention that Serb policemen brought Serbian families to Urosevac, and that they escorted them. Do you know where these families came from? That's my first question. Those Serbian families that had left Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is the following: When I tried to board the train in order to leave Ferizaj, I opened the door to the car and the policeman asked me like, What are you doing? I told him I want to get on. He told me to wait, and at that moment in time I saw Serb families coming off the train. There were men, women, children. I didn't know where they came from. I didn't know them. And after they got off the -- only after they got off the train, we were allowed to board it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that that is quite normal. People need to come out so that people can come in. Now, tell me, please, why did police escort them, accompany them?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I wouldn't be able to tell you. The police were on board when we continued towards Hani i Elezit. They were with us on the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, when you reached the Macedonian border - I'm now speaking of the 16th, the day when you managed to cross into Macedonia, so the 16th of April - did they ask for your IDs, your passports, or any other documents? Did you have to produce those documents at the time? Did the Serbian authorities ask you for that? I'm now referring to police, because police is in charge of checking people's documents when they're crossing border. But it's possible that somebody else could have asked for those documents, say, the army, paramilitaries, anybody else.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody asked us to produce any kinds of documents in the process of crossing into Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not wish to ask you anything else concerning that because you say that nobody confiscated any documents from you. Now, when you reached the boarder, you crossed into Macedonia, and given that on the 15th you didn't manage to enter Macedonia, your colleague Vule, the railway employee who was your friend, told you that you couldn't cross on that day into Macedonia because Macedonian authorities wouldn't let you in. Now, tell me, please, on the following day when you did manage to cross into Macedonia, were you told, were you given any explanation as to why the entry was denied to you on the previous day? I'm now referring to any information that you could have received from the relevant Macedonian authorities.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't inquire as to why we weren't allowed in the day before. We just did not see that kind of argument reasonable. So I don't know why we were accepted and why we were not, so I do not have any further information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is sufficient. Thank you. Mr. Bucaliu, we have heard from you that three Albanian families remained in Staro Selo. Did your mother remain in the village? Your mother who was ill.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained that in my statement but should you see it necessary, I can tell you how my mother was able to make it. She did not stay. After a certain period of time, after 5.00 p.m., she was able to flee the village. At that time my father was not in, however, after I left the village, I met my father at the entrance to Ferizaj. I told him what had happened. I told him that mother had been imploring me to tell her to return and stay with her because she cannot walk and get out, but my father had -- regardless of the difficulty, he wanted to stay with his life-long partner. So he returned and stayed in the village. I told my father to go and besiege of his Serbian friend to transport them with his vehicle out of the village, perhaps tell them that she's ill and she needs to see the doctor. So that's what my father did. He went to the next door neighbour and asked him two or three times, but this neighbour said please do not do this to me, I could not, I could be killed myself if I were to do this. So he didn't do anything. In the meantime, my brother, who alongside 25 other people who were opening those trenches, returned after 5.00 when they were allowed by the forces to do that. So my brother managed to get home. And when he saw that nobody was there, just my mother, he inquired as to what had happened. My mother explained to him. At the time, there was another of my uncles present as well as Hadja, Imam, and his wife. In addition to another elderly woman who was disabled and couldn't walk. So in sum there were six people present over there. There was no other option left. But my brother Fadil was ordered by my father to start the tractor, which they did; they boarded the tractor and they were able in the evening hours to be able, my mother, my brother, and my mother -- and my father, forgive me, to flee the village. So they were able to flee with that tractor. That's what I heard. I didn't meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But you certainly talked to them. And nobody stopped them from leaving the village, did they? even though as you say, paramilitaries said that nobody could leave the village because they needed them as a shield when NATO infantry arrived, but they let them through on a tractor; right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what's happened. It is true that even at that stage nobody stopped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is quite clear. Now, tell me, please, the ones that remained in the village, did they survive? Did something happen to them?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of those two who had been kidnapped, Hasan, Aslan, and their wives, as well as one of my neighbours Fehmi and his wife - who, as I said, the Zeka family -- the four Zeka family members were found massacred in the Prelez neighbourhood. Then Fehmi and his wife who lived next to my Serbian neighbour and who had promised that he would look after them, if we were there nothing was going to happen to them and so on and so forth, but we found them burned inside their own house, i.e., we found parts of their skeleton, their bones, you know, charred in the house. I'm talking about Fehmi and his own wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the people who remained in the village after your departure. When I say "your" I mean the entire village, the entire village which left. Now, those that remained - and there were 30 to 40 of them, in total, three families - did any of them come to any harm after your departure? I'm just asking about those who remained, I'm not asking about the Zeka family, we've heard everything about them. And this other man and his wife, you talked about that as well. I'm just asking about people who remained after your departure. And as far as I could gather, those were the families who lived in the part called Prelez who were apparently very close to those Serbian paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat. After we left, Fehmi, who was very old, and his wife also stayed behind. The others all survive; they live to this day. With the exception of Fehmi and his wife, and the four Zekas, they are also part of that group that stayed behind, we found Fehmi and his wife burned to death in their own houses. And this was three or four months after the war when we returned, so only the charred bodies of these people were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Other than the charred remains, the remains of Fehmi and his wife, do you know anything else about how they lost their lives? Did you hear anything? Because clearly you were not present at the time.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is actually true that we weren't present, all I said is that we found their charred remains. I asked my neighbour who was very, very close, as to what had happened. He declined to tell me. He said, They've set fire to the houses, but I don't know what happened. Even Momir refused to tell me what had happened. Whether he knows or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Momir is your Serb neighbour. I gather that based on his first name. Do you remember his last name?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Momcilo Perovcevic. THE INTERPRETERS: Forgive me. Correction from the interpreter: Tepavcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be kind enough and repeat it clearly, Mr. Bucaliu, because the interpreters didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Momcilo Tepavcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bucaliu, in your statement on the 29th of August, 2001, which also has the date of the 31st of August, 2001, this is your second statement. In paragraph 2 you said that you expected revenge. Why did you expect revenge, or rather, who expected revenge and why? Why did you think that there would be a revenge? What did you have in mind when you said that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I expected it. It actually occurred. We expected some revenge to occur because we knew that Serbian forces would have been unable to withstand a NATO attack and as a result take revenge upon us. And immediately after the NATO air-strikes, the start -- shooting started using the Pragas and this was in the first hour after the NATO bombs started falling. So we had occasion to experience revenge by the Serbian military and paramilitary forces, and this happened on the first night, so revenge started on the very first night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They were attacked by NATO, but why you? Why you?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we were the weaker party. We were on the ground. We were on the ground. The NATO forces were shooting from the air even though the Serbs used their anti-aircraft weapons, they couldn't do anything against them, so they started shooting against us in the [indiscernible]. They often used to say that let the guys from above come to you -- come to save you, and by that they were referring to NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You are Albanians, they are Serbs, but there are also other ethnicities living in Serbia, Ruthenians, Slovaks, Egyptians, and so on. Why would they take revenge against you, Albanians, and not the others? They were attacked by the greatest military power in the world, now why revenge against Albanians? Had Albanians done something evil? What was actually the matter? What would make the Serbs take revenge precisely against Albanians? Because a revenge is taken against the person who has done something to you, so can you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not asserting here that it was only the Albanians who suffered at the hands of Serbian forces. There were others as well. But certainly the Romans, Bosniaks, and there were quite a few amongst them who suffered, so I'm not asserting here that it was only the Albanians who suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's clear. Thank you. Mr. Bucaliu, would you agree with me, you spoke of the 24th of March when the bombing started, and you said that Zika Ilic head of the station told you not to come to work, or, rather, you came to work and he told you you can go back home. And apparently this same thing happened to all other employees. Now would you agree with me that in addition to Albanian employees starting on the 24th of March when the NATO bombing started, many employees, and I'm not referring to railway employees in Urosevac, I'm referring to employees who worked in other companies and institutions and so on. Due to state of war that had been declared immediately left their previous positions and were given other assignments. I'm now referring to the men, and these other assignments had something to do with the state of emergency, state of war, and that most of them were given assignments either with the police, with the army, Territorial Defence, or civilian protection. This applied not only to Albanians but to Serbs and everybody else. Would you agree with me? So not just to Serbs but everybody else you mentioned, Bosniaks, Muslims, Egyptians, Roma?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we were forced out of our jobs. We were not assigned other duties, not in the Territorial Defence or whatever you mentioned, because Albanians were not trusted. And I don't think that there were any Albanians who were part of the civilian or Territorial Defences. We were simply told to leave our jobs. Maybe they didn't even trust us to let us continue with our jobs, but that's exactly what the chief of that station, Zika, told me. He said Albanians can no longer continue working. You can report for work, but you will not be allowed to continue working.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We will agree that the war had begun; right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can say that. If one said that bombing from the air has started, one can easily conclude that war has started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, we go back to what I asked you a bit earlier, why did they mistrust the Albanians at that particular time? I'm not referring to the period ten years prior to that, 20 years prior to that. Why did they not trust Albanians at that particular time? What was the reason? When you say they didn't trust them, you are probably referring to Serbs, the Serbs are the "they." Right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it earlier, that relations between Albanians and the Serbs started cooling down from the 1990s, from the early 1990s. With the forcible constitutional amendments of 1989, i.e., the Constitution of Kosova, the relations started freezing in the ties even and that was noticeable amongst neighbours, amongst colleagues, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, you said that you work at the railroad to this day, that you probably resumed your work there when you came back in July 1999, I assume, and you live nearby your work, but you also said something important that I wish to go back to. You apparently started working in 1987, and you worked all the way up until the day when you met Zika when NATO started bombing and when they told you, From this day on you need not come back to work again. Now, Mr. Bucaliu, in your 1999 statement and also just now, you said that the relations were disrupted between the Serbs and the Albanians, and then you explained this by invoking constitutional amendments. Now, would I be right if I were to say that at least three-quarters of the employees at the railways or railroad was of Albanian ethnicity up until 1999? Would I be right in saying that? You mentioned figures, and now I want you to talk in fractions, I mean, I mentioned three-quarters.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could approximately be true, this figure of three-quarters or a third, or three-quarters, it could be approximately true. So three-quarters were Albanians, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, starting in 1990 onwards, you said that the relations deteriorated, and I see that still the majority of employees were Albanians. Did you and your Albanian colleagues sign some kind of loyalty statements affirming loyalty to the state of Serbia in order to keep their jobs?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, me and my colleagues did not have to sign any loyalty document, and we kept our jobs. We were asked to sign it. We did not -- we were not forced out, but there were other people, however, who were asked to sign it, who refused to do it, and who lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: People who worked at the railway?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. At the directorate level because the main directorate of the railways of Kosova was at Fushe Kosova where a large number of people were employed. So at the central directorate there were, and I could be wrong because a long time had elapsed, there were about 130 people who refused to sign these loyalty documents to the state of Serbia, and these 130 people lost their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Then I can conclude that you did sign such a statement and kept your job. If that was at the level of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not what he said, Mr. Djordjevic. He said he was asked but he was not forced to and he was not removed from his job, but others at a more senior level, at the directorate level, were forced from their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am afraid that there was an interpretation problem. I will have to repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, would I be right in saying that at the directorate level or at the management level of the Kosovo railways, a request came from there for Albanian employees to sign such a statement?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that this request was made, and not only at the directorate level but at every single employee of the railway, so every one of us was requested to sign loyalty to the state of Serbia. But the small stations along the railways did not sign it, and we did not suffer any consequences. At least in the Ferizaj area. Nobody lost their jobs as a result of not signing this statement. However, at the directorate level there were 130 people or more who lost their jobs on account of the fact that they refused to sign this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "at the level of the directorate," you mean only Kosovo Polje, or you mean other towns and cities as well?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only at Kosova Polje at Fushe Kosova because the directorate was stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to stop my cross-examination for the break at this moment and to tender the map that the supplemental witness marked as evidence because now we have a mark C on it. And I would have another half an hour after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned D00128.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While we are correcting, at page 15, line 17 of the transcript appears the phrase "family tree group." It should be paramilitary group. We have, Mr. Djordjevic, been extremely patient with your cross-examination. We have allowed questions that have very little to do with the issues in the case to go unnoticed. It has gone on for a considerable time. We would suggest that you ought to try and finish in no more than a quarter of an hour after we resume. If we are to maintain a reasonable pace with this trial, which I hope you realise is because principally of your client. This trial could be allowed to stretch out for a year and a half or two years, or it could be finished much more quickly. We are trying to finish it as quickly as possible, as long as your client is allowed a proper opportunity to present his Defence. And for that we need the cooperation of counsel, and we need to have the questioning more confined so that it deals only with the important matters. I mentioned this sort of thing several times. I suspect we are going to have to become much more insistent about timing unless counsel respond by being, themselves, much more disciplined in their questions. We will adjourn now and resume at 5 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to stay within the time-limit because I also believe it is in the interests of our client, but of course without infringing on his right to a proper defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, please tell me, what was the level of educational attainment of the employees in the railways in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say, but usually the proper persons were employed at the right post. If a certain post required a high level of education, of course they recruited the relevant person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I wanted to ask you, because you told us that it was always Serbs who occupied managerial positions. Were there any ethnic Albanians in Urosevac who had higher levels of education, who were heads of stations and such?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such persons in Ferizaj. To be a responsible -- to be a manager, you simply had to have a vocational training like the case was with me and some other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mention 1990 as the critical year when the relations between Serbs and Albanians deteriorated. Mr. Bucaliu, was the reason for that the adoption of the new constitution of the Republic of Serbia in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one other reason, reasons. The constitutional amendments that was -- were another reasons for the cooling off of relations. Because after that, some rights that we enjoyed prior to the 1990s were stripped of us after these amendments took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't mind that you make that mistake because you are not a lawyer. It was in fact much earlier than 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask the Trial Chamber, since this has not been admitted yet, that the entire document of the constitution of Serbia from 1990, that's 65 ter number 1021 be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be assigned D00129, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to properly understand what happened and what the witness is talking about, we have to cast our minds back to 1974 when the constitution was in place under which Albanians had much broader rights. Of course, this will be the subject of deliberations of this Trial Chamber, and that's why I would like to tender also the constitution from 1974, which was a federal constitution. 65 ter number 1048. Sorry, 1848. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned D00130.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, did you familiarise yourself in any practical way with the provisions of the constitution from 1974?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, personally I was not familiar with the entire constitution, but Kosova had its own constitution. I'm talking of that constitution and not about the constitution of Serbia or of Yugoslavia. Of course, in relation to some of my personal rights, I had information, but I was talking about the amendment made to the constitution of Kosova. I wasn't talking about the amendments made to the constitution of Serbia, because I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I should not like to debate that with you because you are saying things that are not accurate. Again, I don't mind because you are not a professional. But do you know that the constitution of the Republic of Serbia envisaged Serbo-Croatian as the official language and the official scripts were both Roman and Cyrillic, and that in various republics populated by various nationalities and ethnicities and minorities their languages and their scripts were also in use. And that these languages were equal regardless of ethnicity, that minorities had the right to their language, culture, the use of their script and other rights. Do you know about these provisions when you say that the cooling of relations occurred? These were provisions 8, 32, and 40, from the constitutions of 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we are dealing with a witness who does not claim in any way to be either an expert in law or constitutional law or to be an expert in political affairs. He comes to you telling you simply he is a railway officer. You are not assisting anybody with these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm putting these questions because of the things the witness stated in his statements from 1999 and 2001 when he said he was not allowed to use his own language, and that they were even fined to the tune of 30 per cent to 50 per cent for using the Albanian language. That's why I'm asking him whether he had ever been sanctioned because of this, and what I put to him is the result of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it's going a long way too far. If you want to find from him whether or not he was fined, obviously that's practical. But to debate with him the legality and constitutional propriety of any fine, if there was a fine, is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, you've got about three to four more minutes, so you better use them. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thus the witness was talking about the deteriorating relations between Serbs and Albanians from 1990 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Was he personally ever disciplined in his work organisation, the railway company, for using the Albanian language?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't disciplined myself. But it is a fact that some of my colleagues were deducted a percentage of their salary for using their mother tongue in the place of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that Zika, the chief of the station, called the bus station whenever there was no room in the trains on the 15th and the 16th when you tried to leave for the first time, on the 15th exactly. How do you know that Zika called the buses?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was often present at the train station, and I eye-witnessed when he contacted the police or the bus stations to organise the transport of people, not only by buses but also by trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know about the 15th, that's what I asked. Did you hear that? Did you overhear it?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the 15th I didn't overhear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, my last but one question. Paragraph 17 in your statement, you say that when you finally managed to set out towards Macedonia, that's your 2001 statement, you say the police cordon had been formed so that you could walk only towards the railroad and the border. But in your 1999 statement, you don't mention the cordon, you say that there were policemen who escorted you to the border and told you to follow the railroad because the area around was mined. You say that there were regular army troops around who shouted at you various comments. What -- which one of these is true, the police cordon or army troops shouting various remarks at you?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall to have declared that there was a police line. But there were army officers and soldiers when the train stopped and when we were asked to board off the train, so that is the truth. When we were told to get off, I don't want to repeat myself, there were police and soldiers. I don't think I have said that there was a police line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My reference is paragraph 17 in your statement from 2001, but you've just explained it in such a way that it does not require any more time. Here is my last question regarding the diary kept already in the evidence. On the 24th of March, the air-strikes against Serbia started. Until the 29th of March, not a single train passed, will you agree? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the log-book with me. If there is nothing written, if there is no entry in the log-book about that, then it's true, that no train passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On the day when you first moved, it was entered that there were only two trains. The train you took left at 0817 hours which coincides with other information, and you returned in the afternoon because you did not manage to cross the border. On the 16th there were again two trains, and the train that left to the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing carrying 3.000 people and 10 policemen, you say that it arrived at the time you indicated. But I want to ask you this, and that's my last question, was it customary for policemen it to escort trains, even in peacetime? As a railroad worker, you should know that.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that now and again, not always, I'm talking of local trains that circulated all over Kosova, so there were instances when there were policemen present in the train, but not always. In very rare occasions. And we are talking about one or two police, policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this completes my cross-examination. Thank you for the time you gave me. In the future, I will limit my questions to those directly linked to the case. Mr. Bucaliu, thank you for all the clarifications you've given us. I think this will contribute even more to the establishment of truth and facts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djordjevic. Ms. D'Ascoli, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, you were asked by my learned colleague from the Defence about the Serbs living in your village and whether upon your return to the village they were still there or how -- what happened to their houses. And you said that after June or anyway after you returned to your village the houses were demolished. I was interested in knowing whether upon your return in Staro Selo, you saw what happened to the Serb houses in your village, if you happen to notice that? In which condition you found them.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained earlier when I returned with the exception of one house belonging the the Serbs the others were demolished.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So when you returned they were already demolished?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I understood that they were demolished afterwards. And in which condition did you find your own house?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My house and the houses of my brothers and of many neighbours were completely burned down. Nothing was intact. And this was the case with about 40 houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: What about these 40 houses, were they belonging to your neighbourhood or to which people?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the houses of Albanians. I explained that the Serbs' houses were also demolished, but I'm talking about the houses of Albanians which were burned down by the Serb forces. About the Serb houses, I may presume that most probably they were destroyed by Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bucaliu. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you Ms. D'Ascoli. Mr. Bucaliu, you will be pleased to know that completes the the questions for you. We would like to thank you for your being able to travel to The Hague and for the assistance that you've been able to give us. And you may now of course return to your normal activities. And the court officer will show you out. Thank you indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My thanks to all of you Honourable Judges. I didn't have an opportunity to go into details about one aspect because there were some things which were not clear in other transcripts or trials about why trains came there, why they were not stopped or stopped. If you want further details, I may explain it to you, if you can give me 5 minutes, if that is of relevance to you. If not, then I'm content as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for your offer, but I believe we've got the information we need. So thank you indeed. The court officer will show you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Now that this witness went out, I would like to ask you for an explanation. The next witness has protective measures. I think that we are going to have a closed session. I will need to put to this witness a statement of another protected witness who also testified in closed session. Now, could you now give me instructions as to how to do this best. Should I mention the position of the previous protected witness? Now, if I mention the position and the function that he held then everybody will know his identity, even though it's a closed session, or should I only refer to that other protected witness by pseudonym? And it has do with some contradictory statements of these two protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have a statement or a transcript of this other witness that you need to put to the person here? So you'll need to show him a document or more than one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First I can just put a question to him and say another witness said this or that, or I can show him a portion of the transcript, since I have it on the list of documents I wish to use. But I'm not going to use it, if it is contrary to the rules of procedure, or perhaps you can instruct me as to how to use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a matter of degree and necessity. If it's possible to effectively conduct your cross-examination without identifying a protected witness to this witness, that should be done. So that if you can say to him, I want you to comment on the evidence given by another person in this trial or in another trial where that person said this, this, this, and this, and you quote, that will usually be effective and enough. If for some reason that isn't working, we may have to make some other special procedural provision. But perhaps you could try that approach to begin with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm taking a guess at Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct. The next witness is K-86, but since it's closed session I was wondering if it might be convenient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well we're about to do that now if that is the witness, and you are about to move into a better position, and we'll move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 28th of May, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
